summary: CCC-built ground-mounted L-4 cab in the Frank Church Wilderness, abandoned for years, hike-in only, re-roofed by volunteers in 2014-2015.

facts.design: ground-mounted L-4 standard cab, a 1930s design
facts.status_note: Described as abandoned for years. Volunteers re-roofed it in 2014 or 2015, depending on the source.

access.note: Hike-in only, inside the Frank Church River of No Return Wilderness. No source reports a closure.

visit.trail_note: Hike-in only per Idaho Fire Lookouts; no trail length given.

facts.agency: US Forest Service - Boise National Forest

events.note: Ground-mounted L-4 cab built by the Civilian Conservation Corps. Forest Lookouts and firelookout.com give 1934.
Fire guards at the station in August 1936, quoted by Forest Lookouts from The Salt Lake Tribune
Supply drop from an airplane landed on the station stove, breaking the window and the stove
Roof replaced and some paint work done by Treasure Valley Back Country Horsemen, per NHLR and Idaho Fire Lookouts. Forest Lookouts dates the completed re-roof to 2015.
Shingles flown to the Middle Fork of the Salmon River and packed to the lookout for storage. Heritage Trust grant year 2014.
Re-roofing completed in August 2015, per Forest Lookouts
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register, October 3, 2020

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR, Idaho Heritage Trust and Idaho Fire Lookouts give 1933. Forest Lookouts and firelookout.com give 1934. The story uses 1933 and notes the disagreement.
NHLR and Idaho Fire Lookouts date the roof replacement to 2014. Forest Lookouts says the shingles were packed in during 2014 and the re-roof was completed in August 2015. The story reports both.
NHLR names Boise National Forest. firelookout.com and Idaho Fire Lookouts name Boise/Challis National Forests. The story uses the NHLR name.

notes_for_editor: Record status 'standing' is kept, but every source describes the site as abandoned for years and no recent condition report was found. Build year (1933 vs 1934) and roof year (2014 vs 2015) are both disputed across sources. The 1936 anecdote is a reprint on Forest Lookouts of a Salt Lake Tribune item; the original newspaper was not checked. Access is set to public (wilderness hike-in); no closure reported.
